title: Do you need an LLC to freelance in the US?
summary: Do I need an LLC to freelance in the US? Compare liability, tax and setup cost against staying a sole proprietor. Get the full breakdown first.
body_markdown:
An old classmate of mine started freelancing in the US a couple of years ago. At first, it was a few small projects, and he got paid in his personal account, with nothing formal in place. He’s always had a great work ethic, so it wasn’t surprising to see his business take on getting steady clients, bigger contracts, and subsequently, a large, sustainable income that had grown massively.


During one of our catch-up calls, I got to understand that, as a sole proprietor, his business and personal finances are legally one and the same, so a dispute or debt on the business side could generally reach his personal savings. He’d been thinking about whether he needed an LLC. We researched together and found that the answer depended on his risk, income, and his clients, not on a legal rule.


This guide details our findings and covers what an LLC does, what it costs, and when it’s worth forming.


Typically, you don’t need an LLC to freelance in the US. Most freelancers start as sole proprietors and can work legally without one. You should consider an LLC once you want liability protection, have more to lose, or want a more professional setup. It generally separates your personal and business assets.


## Do freelancers need an LLC?


No. You do not need an LLC to freelance in the US. If you do freelance work without registering any other business structure, you are automatically treated as a sole proprietor.


That is the default for most freelancers, and it is simple. There is no formation filing, no separate business entity, and no annual state fee to maintain one. Your business income is reported on your personal tax return, and you pay self-employment tax on your profits.


The trade-off is that a sole proprietorship is not separate from you. The SBA says sole proprietors can be held personally liable for the business’s debts and obligations. If a client sues you or a business debt goes unpaid, your personal savings and property may be exposed.


Being a sole proprietor does not mean you can ignore the paperwork. Depending on your city, state, and line of work, you may still need a business licence or permit, and you may need to register a trade name if you work under a name other than your own. Check with your state and local offices.


For a side-by-side look at the two options, read our guide to[LLC vs sole proprietorship](https://grey.co/blog/llc-vs-sole-proprietorship) . If you are new to the default option, we also explain[what a sole proprietorship is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-sole-proprietorship) .


## Benefits of an LLC for freelancers


The main benefit of an LLC for a freelancer is liability protection: it creates a separate legal entity, so your personal assets are generally shielded from the business’s debts and lawsuits. That is not the only advantage. Here are the benefits worth weighing:


- **Liability protection**
The SBA says LLCs protect you from personal liability in most instances, so your personal assets are generally not at risk if the LLC is sued or cannot pay its debts. The protection has limits. It does not usually cover debts you personally guaranteed, fraud, or your own wrongful acts. Professional insurance is a separate layer of protection, and many freelancers use it with or without an LLC.
- **Separate business and personal money**
An LLC gives you a reason to run a dedicated business bank account, which makes your records cleaner at tax time. Keeping the two apart is also generally expected if you want the liability protection to hold up.
- **Credibility**
“Jane Doe Design LLC” immediately looks more established to some clients than an individual name, and some larger clients prefer to contract with a registered business.
- **Simple pass-through taxation by default**
The SBA says LLC profits and losses can pass through to your personal income without facing corporate taxes. For income tax purposes, the IRS treats a single-member LLC as a disregarded entity separate from its owner unless it elects otherwise.
- **Tax options later**
An LLC can file Form 8832 to elect to be taxed as a corporation, and a qualifying LLC can elect S corporation status. These elections change how the business is taxed and add filing requirements, so they are worth discussing with a tax professional before you commit. See the[IRS guidance on LLCs filing as a corporation or partnership](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/llc-filing-as-a-corporation-or-partnership) .


One thing an LLC does not do by default is cut your tax bill. The SBA notes that LLC members are considered self-employed and pay self-employment tax contributions toward Social Security and Medicare, just as sole proprietors do.


## Downsides and costs


The main downsides of an LLC are the costs and the admin: you pay a state filing fee to form it, and most states charge fees or taxes to keep it active. Weigh these against the benefits above:


- **Filing fees:** Every state charges a fee to form an LLC, and the amount varies widely.
- **Ongoing costs:** Many states require an annual or biennial report, and some charge a yearly fee or tax on top.
- **More paperwork:** You need a registered agent, a filing with your state, and, in many cases, an operating agreement. You also need to keep business and personal money apart.
- **No automatic tax savings:** A single-member LLC is taxed like a sole proprietorship by default, and self-employment tax still applies.
- **Protection is not absolute:** Personal guarantees, fraud, and your own wrongful acts can still put your personal assets at risk.


Costs depend heavily on where you form the LLC. These examples come from state agencies, and you should check the current figures before you file:


- **Wyoming:** a $100 filing fee for Articles of Organisation, and an annual report fee that starts at $60.
- **Florida:** $125 to file, made up of a $100 filing fee and a $25 registered agent designation fee, plus a $138.75 annual report.
- **Texas:** a $300 filing fee for the certificate of formation.
- **California:** an $800 annual tax for every LLC doing business or organised in the state, and an extra fee once California income passes $250,000. The[California Franchise Tax Board](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/business/types/limited-liability-company/index.html) sets out the details.


The gap between states can be large. A freelancer in a low-fee state pays far less to keep an LLC than one in a state with a high annual tax, and an LLC formed in one state may need to register in another if you work from there. For a state-by-state breakdown, see our guide to[how much it costs to start an LLC](https://grey.co/blog/how-much-does-llc-cost) .


## When should a freelancer form an LLC?


A freelancer should form an LLC when the risk of losing personal assets or of a client’s requirements outweighs the yearly cost of maintaining one. If you are asking at what income level you need an LLC, there is no income threshold that makes one mandatory. It is a judgment about risk, not a legal threshold.


These signs suggest it may be time:


- **You have more to protect:** A home, savings, or other assets are all exposed if you are sued or owe a business debt as a sole proprietor.
- **Your work carries real risk:** If a mistake could cost a client a lot of money or cause injury or damage, the stakes rise.
- **Your clients are getting bigger:** Larger clients may prefer or require a registered business, and their contracts often carry more liability.
- **You are hiring or subcontracting:** Working with other people adds risk and paperwork.
- **You are taking on debt or signing leases:.** Contracts like these are where limited liability matters most.
- **Your income is steady:** If the business is no longer a side project, the annual cost is easier to justify.


There are also good reasons to wait. If you are just starting out, earn little, do low-risk work, or live in a state with a high annual tax, staying a sole proprietor and using clear written contracts may be enough. Many freelancers start that way and convert later.


The SBA’s guide to[choosing a business structure](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business/choose-business-structure) is a useful starting point. It notes that ownership rules, liability, taxes, and filing requirements vary by state, and that LLCs can have a limited life in many states, so check the rules where you live.


*This is general guidance, not professional tax advice. Consult a certified tax professional for your specific situation. It is also not legal advice, so speak to a qualified lawyer about your liability.*


## Getting paid as a freelancer


Whatever structure you choose, you get paid by sending clear invoices and giving clients an easy way to pay. Both matter more when your clients are overseas.


Start with the paperwork. A written agreement that sets out the scope, rate, due date, and payment method prevents most disputes. Our guide to[writing a freelance contract](https://grey.co/blog/freelance-contract-guide) covers the key clauses. On each invoice, state the currency, the due date, and exactly how the client should pay.

## Frequently asked questions


### Do I need an LLC to freelance?


No. You can legally freelance in the US as a sole proprietor without forming a business entity. An LLC is optional and mainly adds liability protection.


### When should I form one?


Form an LLC when the risk of losing personal assets or a client's requirements outweighs the annual cost of maintaining one. Common triggers are bigger clients, higher-risk work, hiring help, signing leases or taking on debt, and having more assets to protect.


### How much does an LLC cost?


It depends on the state. For example, Wyoming charges $100 to form an LLC and at least $60 for its annual report, while Florida charges $125 to form one and $138.75 for the annual report. California charges every LLC an $800 annual tax. Check your state's Secretary of State for current fees.


### Can I freelance as a sole proprietor?


Yes. If you do freelance work without registering another structure, you are a sole proprietor by default. You may still need a local business licence or permit, and you are personally liable for business debts.


### Does an LLC save tax?


Not by itself. A single-member LLC is taxed like a sole proprietorship by default, and self-employment tax still applies. An LLC can elect corporate or S corporation treatment, which may change your tax, so speak to a tax professional first.


### How do I get paid by overseas clients?


Agree on the currency and payment method in your contract, then state them on every invoice. Clients can pay by bank transfer, and a multi-currency account such as Grey's can provide a place to receive and hold the funds. Check the rate and fee before you move it.
